problems.title: Lorentz factor at a stated speed
problems.objective: Analyze lorentz factor at a stated speed with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: A spacecraft moves at $0.800c$ relative to an inertial laboratory. Find its Lorentz factor $\gamma$.
problems.strategy: First: Write $\beta=v/c$ before evaluating the factor. Next: Use $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. Finally: Check that the result exceeds one and grows with speed.
hints: Write $\beta=v/c$ before evaluating the factor.
Check that the result exceeds one and grows with speed.
rubricCriteria: Correctly completes the setup: Write $\beta=v/c$ before evaluating the factor.
Correctly carries out the central step: Use $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$.
Completes and checks the result: Check that the result exceeds one and grows with speed.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\gamma=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The Lorentz factor is the reciprocal square root and must exceed one for nonzero speed.

commonErrors.description: Treats $0.800c$ as $0.800\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The quoted number is a fraction of the invariant light speed.

problems.solution: $\beta=0.800$, so $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.800^2}=1/0.600=1.667$. The value is dimensionless and greater than one.
problems.flawedProof: $\gamma=\sqrt{1-0.800^2}=0.600$, so moving clocks run faster by a factor below one.

problems.title: Dilated lifetime in the laboratory
problems.objective: Analyze dilated lifetime in the laboratory with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: An unstable particle has proper lifetime $2.20\,\mu\mathrm s$ and moves at $0.600c$ in a laboratory. Find its mean lifetime measured by laboratory clocks.
problems.strategy: First: Identify the particle-frame lifetime as the proper time. Next: Evaluate $\gamma$ at $0.600c$ and multiply the proper lifetime. Finally: Check that the laboratory lifetime is longer.
permittedResults: $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ for a clock moving between the two events.
hints: Identify the particle-frame lifetime as the proper time.
Evaluate $\gamma$ at $0.600c$ and multiply the proper lifetime.
Check that the laboratory lifetime is longer.
rubricCriteria: Correctly completes the setup: Identify the particle-frame lifetime as the proper time.
Correctly carries out the central step: Evaluate $\gamma$ at $0.600c$ and multiply the proper lifetime.
Completes and checks the result: Check that the laboratory lifetime is longer.

commonErrors.description: Divides the proper lifetime by $\gamma$.
commonErrors.consequence: Time dilation makes the coordinate time between ticks larger than the proper time.

commonErrors.description: Calls the laboratory time the proper time.
commonErrors.consequence: The two events occur at the same place only in the particle rest frame.

problems.solution: $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.600^2}=1.25$. Hence $\Delta t=(1.25)(2.20\,\mu\mathrm s)=2.75\,\mu\mathrm s$, longer than the proper lifetime.
problems.flawedProof: $\Delta t=\Delta\tau/\gamma=2.20/1.25=1.76\,\mu\mathrm s$ because motion shortens every measured interval.

problems.title: Contracted length of a moving rod
problems.objective: Analyze contracted length of a moving rod with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: A rod has rest length $5.00\,\mathrm m$ and moves parallel to its length at $0.800c$. Find its length measured simultaneously in the laboratory.
problems.strategy: First: Identify $5.00\,\mathrm m$ as the proper length. Next: Use the laboratory Lorentz factor for the rod. Finally: Divide by $\gamma$ and check that the moving length is shorter.

Use the laboratory Lorentz factor for the rod.

commonErrors.description: Multiplies the rest length by $\gamma$.
commonErrors.consequence: A length parallel to the motion is contracted, not enlarged.

commonErrors.description: Omits the simultaneity condition on endpoint positions.
commonErrors.consequence: A frame-specific length requires endpoint coordinates at one time in that frame.

problems.solution: $\gamma=1.667$, so $L=5.00/1.667=3.00\,\mathrm m$. The laboratory must record the endpoint positions simultaneously in that frame.
problems.flawedProof: $L=\gamma L_0=(1.667)(5.00)=8.33\,\mathrm m$ because all moving spatial dimensions are dilated.

problems.title: Simultaneity depends on the inertial frame
problems.objective: Analyze simultaneity depends on the inertial frame with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: Two flashes occur simultaneously in a laboratory at positions separated along the $x$ direction. A second inertial frame moves in the $+x$ direction. Must the flashes be simultaneous in the second frame? State the sign of $\Delta t^{\prime}$ when $\Delta x>0$.
problems.strategy: First: Set $\Delta t=0$ in the laboratory. Next: Apply the Lorentz transformation for the time separation. Finally: Use the signs of $v$ and $\Delta x$ to determine event order.
hints: Set $\Delta t=0$ in the laboratory.

commonErrors.consequence: The spacetime interval is invariant; a zero coordinate-time separation for spatially separated events is not.

commonErrors.description: Drops the spatial term in the time transformation.
commonErrors.consequence: Separated simultaneous events acquire a nonzero transformed time difference.

problems.solution: They need not be simultaneous. With $v>0$, $\Delta x>0$, and $\Delta t=0$, $\Delta t^{\prime}=-\gamma v\Delta x/c^2<0$. The event at larger $x$ occurs earlier in the moving frame.
problems.flawedProof: Both observers see light travel at $c$, so two simultaneous flashes must remain simultaneous and $\Delta t^{\prime}=0$.

problems.title: Light speed survives velocity transformation

problems.statement: Frame $S^{\prime}$ moves at speed $v$ along $+x$ relative to $S$. A light pulse moves at $u_x=c$ in $S$. Use the collinear velocity transformation to find $u_x^{\prime}$.
problems.strategy: First: Insert $u_x=c$ into the velocity transformation. Next: Factor the same term from numerator and denominator. Finally: State the result without using Galilean subtraction.

commonErrors.consequence: The dimensionless term is $u_xv/c^2$.

problems.flawedProof: $u_x^{\prime}=c-v$ because the moving observer simply subtracts its own speed from the pulse speed.

problems.objective: Analyze muon survival through the atmosphere with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: Muons have proper mean lifetime $2.20\,\mu\mathrm s$ and travel at $0.998c$ toward Earth. In the Earth frame, find their mean travel distance before decay. Ignore energy loss.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the Lorentz factor at $0.998c$. Next: Dilate the proper lifetime in the Earth frame. Finally: Multiply the Earth-frame lifetime by the Earth-frame speed.
permittedResults: $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$ and distance equals speed times coordinate time.
hints: Compute the Lorentz factor at $0.998c$.
Dilate the proper lifetime in the Earth frame.
Multiply the Earth-frame lifetime by the Earth-frame speed.

problems.strategy: First: Compute $\gamma$ for the cruise speed. Next: Contract the planet separation into the ship frame. Finally: Divide that separation by the planet speed in the ship frame.

problems.title: Classical limit of relativistic kinetic energy

commonErrors.description: Demands that both frames agree the two doors close simultaneously.
commonErrors.consequence: Simultaneity of spatially separated door events is frame dependent.

commonErrors.description: Contracts both pole and barn in the barn frame.
commonErrors.consequence: Only the moving pole is length contracted in that frame.

problems.solution: At $0.800c$, $\gamma=1.667$, so the pole length in the barn frame is $6.00\,\mathrm m<7.00\,\mathrm m$ and both doors can close simultaneously there. In the pole frame the barn is contracted, but the separated door-closing events have $\Delta t^{\prime}\ne0$; the front door closes and reopens before the rear door closes, so the pole is never trapped by simultaneous closures in its frame.
problems.flawedProof: Because both doors close simultaneously in the barn frame, they must also close simultaneously in the pole frame, creating a contradiction.

problems.title: Derive velocity addition and preserve the speed limit
problems.objective: Analyze derive velocity addition and preserve the speed limit with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: Starting from the differential Lorentz transformation for a boost along $x$, derive the transformation of $u_x=dx/dt$ to $u_x^{\prime}$. Then prove that $|u_x|<c$ and $|v|<c$ imply $|u_x^{\prime}|<c$.
problems.strategy: First: Divide $dx^{\prime}$ by $dt^{\prime}$ using the transformed differentials. Next: Simplify to the rational velocity formula. Finally: Factor $1-u_x^{\prime2}/c^2$ to prove positivity.

commonErrors.description: Argues only from one numerical example.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested speed-limit statement requires an algebraic inequality for all subluminal inputs.

problems.solution: $u_x^{\prime}=(dx-vdt)/(dt-vdx/c^2)=(u_x-v)/(1-u_xv/c^2)$. Direct algebra gives $1-u_x^{\prime2}/c^2=[(1-u_x^2/c^2)(1-v^2/c^2)]/(1-u_xv/c^2)^2>0$, so $|u_x^{\prime}|<c$.

commonErrors.description: Sets all final particles at rest in the laboratory.

problems.solution: With $P=P_1+P_2$, $(P-P_1)^2=P_2^2$. In the parent rest frame this gives $M^2c^2+m_1^2c^2-2ME_1=m_2^2c^2$. Therefore $E_1=[M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2]c^2/(2M)$.

problems.solution: $\eta_1=\operatorname{artanh}(0.100)=0.100335$. Thus $\eta_{10}=1.00335$ and $\beta_{10}=\tanh(1.00335)=0.763$. The Galilean sum is $1.00c$, while the relativistic result remains subluminal.

problems.title: Worldline under constant proper acceleration

commonErrors.description: Omits the offset in the hyperbola.
commonErrors.consequence: The chosen initial condition $x=0$ requires $x+c^2/a$ in the invariant relation.

problems.solution: Integration from zero gives the stated $t(\tau)$ and $x(\tau)$. Since $x+c^2/a=(c^2/a)\cosh(a\tau/c)$ and $ct=(c^2/a)\sinh(a\tau/c)$, $(x+c^2/a)^2-c^2t^2=(c^2/a)^2$. For small $\tau$, $t\approx\tau$ and $x\approx a\tau^2/2\approx at^2/2$.

problems.solution: $E_{\mathrm{tot}}=10.0\,\mathrm{GeV}$ and $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=4.00\,\mathrm{GeV}/c$. Hence $v_{\mathrm{CM}}=0.400c$ along $+x$. Also $Mc^2=\sqrt{10.0^2-4.00^2}\,\mathrm{GeV}=\sqrt{84}=9.17\,\mathrm{GeV}$.

problems.title: Relativistic elastic collision with equal masses
problems.objective: Analyze relativistic elastic collision with equal masses with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: In one dimension, a particle of mass $m$ and speed $u$ strikes an identical particle initially at rest. Show that the only elastic final states are the unchanged state or exchange of velocities. Assume both particles remain identical and no other products appear.
problems.strategy: First: Write conservation of total momentum and total relativistic energy. Next: Use rapidity or strict convexity of $E(p)=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$. Finally: Identify the two permutations of the initial momenta.
permittedResults: Relativistic energy is $E(p)=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$ and is strictly convex in one dimension.
hints: Write conservation of total momentum and total relativistic energy.
Use rapidity or strict convexity of $E(p)=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$.
Identify the two permutations of the initial momenta.

Correctly carries out the central step: Use rapidity or strict convexity of $E(p)=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$.

commonErrors.description: Uses only momentum conservation to claim infinitely many elastic outcomes.
commonErrors.consequence: Elasticity also imposes total relativistic energy conservation.

commonErrors.description: Assumes Newtonian kinetic energy in the proof.
commonErrors.consequence: The conclusion holds, but the requested relativistic derivation must use $E(p)$.

problems.solution: Let initial momenta be $(p,0)$ and final momenta $(q,p-q)$. Energy conservation requires $E(p)+E(0)=E(q)+E(p-q)$. For fixed sum $p$, strict convexity and symmetry make the equality occur at the endpoint permutations $q=p$ or $q=0$. Thus the particles either pass through unchanged or exchange velocities, physically indistinguishable for identical particles.
problems.flawedProof: Momentum conservation alone gives $p=q+(p-q)$ for every $q$, so every pair of final velocities is elastic.

problems.title: Minimum photon energy in a moving frame
problems.objective: Analyze minimum photon energy in a moving frame with explicit inertial frames and assumptions, consistent relativistic signs and units, and a limiting or invariant check.
problems.statement: A photon has energy $E$ in $S$ and travels at angle $\theta$ from the $+x$ axis. Frame $S^{\prime}$ moves at speed $v$ along $+x$. Derive $E^{\prime}$ and, for fixed $v$ and $E$, find the propagation direction that minimizes it.

Factor out $E$ and express the result with $\beta$.
Minimize the linear dependence on $\cos\theta$ over its allowed interval.
rubricCriteria: Correctly completes the setup: Use $p_x=(E/c)\cos\theta$ in the energy boost.
Correctly carries out the central step: Factor out $E$ and express the result with $\beta$.
Completes and checks the result: Minimize the linear dependence on $\cos\theta$ over its allowed interval.

commonErrors.description: Minimizes the energy for a head-on photon with $\cos\theta=-1$.
commonErrors.consequence: A head-on photon is blueshifted; chasing a forward photon gives the redshift minimum.

commonErrors.description: Transforms photon energy as $E/\gamma$ independent of angle.
commonErrors.consequence: A boost mixes energy with the momentum component along the boost.

problems.solution: $E^{\prime}=\gamma E(1-\beta\cos\theta)$. For $\beta>0$, this is minimized by $\cos\theta=1$, a photon traveling in the same $+x$ direction as the moving frame. The minimum is $E_{\min}^{\prime}=\gamma E(1-\beta)=E\sqrt{(1-\beta)/(1+\beta)}$.
problems.flawedProof: The photon energy is smallest for $\theta=\pi$ because opposite directions cancel, giving $E^{\prime}=\gamma E(1+\beta)$.

Their opposite momenta have magnitude $p=\frac{c}{2M}\sqrt{[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2][M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2]}$, equivalently $pc=\frac{c^2}{2M}\sqrt{[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2][M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2]}$. commonErrors.consequence: The nanometre conversion is omitted, making both frequency and energy wrong by nine powers of ten.

commonErrors.description: Multiplying the joule value by $1.602\times10^{-19}$ converts it to electronvolts.
commonErrors.consequence: The joule-to-electronvolt conversion must divide by the joules in one electronvolt.

problems.solution: $\lambda=5.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm m$, so $f=(2.998\times10^8)/(5.00\times10^{-7})=5.996\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Then $E=hf=3.973\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm J=2.480\,\mathrm{eV}$. This is the expected few-electronvolt scale for visible light, and $E\propto1/\lambda$.
problems.flawedProof: I substitute $\lambda=500\,\mathrm m$ directly, so $f=c/\lambda=5.996\times10^5\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $E=hf=3.97\times10^{-28}\,\mathrm J$. Therefore the photon has an extremely small energy.

problems.title: Electron de Broglie wavelength
problems.objective: Analyze electron de broglie wavelength from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: An electron moves nonrelativistically at $2.00\times10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find its de Broglie wavelength. Use $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $h=6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, and verify that the nonrelativistic assumption is reasonable.
problems.strategy: First: Use the nonrelativistic momentum $p=m_ev$. Next: Substitute into $\lambda=h/p$ with SI units. Finally: Compare $v$ with $c$ and check that the wavelength is on an atomic scale.
hints: Use the nonrelativistic momentum $p=m_ev$.
Substitute into $\lambda=h/p$ with SI units.
Compare $v$ with $c$ and check that the wavelength is on an atomic scale.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use the nonrelativistic momentum $p=m_ev$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Substitute into $\lambda=h/p$ with SI units.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Compare $v$ with $c$ and check that the wavelength is on an atomic scale.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\lambda=hv/m_e$ instead of $h/(m_ev)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The expression is dimensionally wrong and predicts wavelength increasing with momentum.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that every electron calculation must be relativistic because electrons are elementary particles.
commonErrors.consequence: Relativity is controlled by $v/c$, not by whether a particle is elementary.

problems.solution: $p=(9.109\times10^{-31})(2.00\times10^6)=1.822\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$, hence $\lambda=6.626\times10^{-34}/(1.822\times10^{-24})=3.64\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m=0.364\,\mathrm{nm}$. Since $v/c=6.67\times10^{-3}$, the nonrelativistic approximation is excellent; the wavelength is comparable with atomic spacings.
problems.flawedProof: Starting from $\lambda=h/p$, I move $v$ to the numerator and write $\lambda=hv/m_e$. Substitution gives $\lambda=(6.626\times10^{-34})(2.00\times10^6)/(9.109\times10^{-31})=1.45\times10^3\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: Probability in a normalized interval state
problems.objective: Analyze probability in a normalized interval state from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A normalized one-dimensional wavefunction is $\psi(x)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(\pi x/L)$ for $0<x<L$ and zero elsewhere. Without integrating, find the probability of detecting the particle somewhere in $0<x<L$, and state what quantity is the probability density.
problems.strategy: First: Use the statement that the wavefunction is normalized over all space. Next: Identify the support of $\psi$ and apply $P=\int |\psi|^2dx$. Finally: Distinguish the amplitude $\psi$ from the nonnegative density $|\psi|^2$.
hints: Use the statement that the wavefunction is normalized over all space.
Identify the support of $\psi$ and apply $P=\int |\psi|^2dx$.
Distinguish the amplitude $\psi$ from the nonnegative density $|\psi|^2$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use the statement that the wavefunction is normalized over all space.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Identify the support of $\psi$ and apply $P=\int |\psi|^2dx$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Distinguish the amplitude $\psi$ from the nonnegative density $|\psi|^2$.

commonErrors.description: Treats $\psi(x)$ itself as the probability density and integrates the amplitude rather than its modulus squared.
commonErrors.consequence: The Born density is $|\psi|^2$; integrating the amplitude does not produce the probability measure.

commonErrors.description: The total probability is $L$ because the allowed interval has length $L$.
commonErrors.consequence: Probability follows from integrating the normalized density, not from interval length alone.

problems.solution: The wavefunction vanishes outside $(0,L)$ and is normalized over all space, so $P(0<x<L)=1$. The probability density is $|\psi(x)|^2=(2/L)\sin^2(\pi x/L)$ in the interval and zero outside. It has units of inverse length, so its integral is dimensionless.
problems.flawedProof: Because $\psi(x)$ is normalized, I use $\psi(x)$ itself as the probability density. Thus the probability in the box is $\int_0^L\psi(x)dx=2\sqrt{2L}/\pi$, rather than an integral of $|\psi|^2$.

problems.title: Hydrogen photon from an energy gap
problems.objective: Analyze hydrogen photon from an energy gap from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A hydrogen atom drops from an energy level at $-3.40\,\mathrm{eV}$ to one at $-13.60\,\mathrm{eV}$. Find the emitted photon energy and state why its energy is positive.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the atomic change $\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}=E_f-E_i$. Next: Use energy conservation so that $E_\gamma=-\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}$ for emission. Finally: Check that the atom loses energy while the photon carries a positive energy.
hints: Compute the atomic change $\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}=E_f-E_i$.
Use energy conservation so that $E_\gamma=-\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}$ for emission.
Check that the atom loses energy while the photon carries a positive energy.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Compute the atomic change $\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}=E_f-E_i$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Use energy conservation so that $E_\gamma=-\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}$ for emission.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the atom loses energy while the photon carries a positive energy.

commonErrors.description: Reports $E_\gamma=E_f-E_i=-10.20\,\mathrm{eV}$.
commonErrors.consequence: Photon energy cannot be negative; the negative number is the atom's energy change.

commonErrors.description: Adds the magnitudes $3.40+13.60$ and obtains $17.00\,\mathrm{eV}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy released is the difference between levels, not the sum of their binding-energy magnitudes.

problems.solution: $\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}=-13.60-(-3.40)=-10.20\,\mathrm{eV}$. Conservation of energy gives $E_\gamma=-\Delta E_{\mathrm{atom}}=10.20\,\mathrm{eV}$. The atom's energy decreases, while the emitted photon necessarily has positive energy.
problems.flawedProof: The photon energy is the final atomic energy minus the initial energy: $E_\gamma=E_f-E_i=-13.60-(-3.40)=-10.20\,\mathrm{eV}$. I therefore report an emitted photon energy of $-10.20\,\mathrm{eV}$.

problems.title: Uncertainty is not instrument damage
problems.objective: Analyze uncertainty is not instrument damage from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A student says, ‘A sufficiently gentle microscope could reveal an electron's exact position and momentum simultaneously; present uncertainty is only experimental disturbance.’ Decide whether this claim is consistent with quantum mechanics and identify the relevant bound.
problems.strategy: First: Interpret $\Delta x$ and $\Delta p_x$ as statistical spreads in a quantum state. Next: Apply the state-independent bound $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$. Finally: Explain why improved apparatus cannot prepare a state with both spreads equal to zero.
hints: Interpret $\Delta x$ and $\Delta p_x$ as statistical spreads in a quantum state.
Apply the state-independent bound $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$.
Explain why improved apparatus cannot prepare a state with both spreads equal to zero.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Interpret $\Delta x$ and $\Delta p_x$ as statistical spreads in a quantum state.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Apply the state-independent bound $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Explain why improved apparatus cannot prepare a state with both spreads equal to zero.

commonErrors.description: The bound disappears when the measuring instrument does not disturb the electron.
commonErrors.consequence: The uncertainty relation constrains state spreads even before any particular measurement protocol is chosen.

commonErrors.description: The relation says every individual measurement result has an experimental error of at least $\hbar/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The product concerns standard deviations of repeated measurements, not a product of two single-shot instrument errors.

problems.solution: The claim is inconsistent with quantum mechanics. The quantities $\Delta x$ and $\Delta p_x$ are intrinsic standard deviations for ensembles prepared in the same state, and they obey $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$. Instrument disturbance can add error, but eliminating that error cannot make both intrinsic spreads vanish.
problems.flawedProof: The uncertainty product comes entirely from disturbing the electron during measurement. With an ideally gentle apparatus the disturbance is zero, so one may take $\Delta x=\Delta p_x=0$ and know both quantities exactly.

problems.title: Photoelectric threshold decision
problems.objective: Analyze photoelectric threshold decision from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A metal has work function $2.30\,\mathrm{eV}$. It is illuminated separately by photons of energy $2.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $2.70\,\mathrm{eV}$. State whether photoelectrons are emitted in each case and, when they are, give the maximum kinetic energy.
problems.strategy: First: Compare each photon energy with the work function $\phi$. Next: For an allowed event use $K_{\max}=E_\gamma-\phi$; below threshold there is no emission. Finally: Check that kinetic energy is never assigned a negative physical value.
hints: Compare each photon energy with the work function $\phi$.
For an allowed event use $K_{\max}=E_\gamma-\phi$; below threshold there is no emission.
Check that kinetic energy is never assigned a negative physical value.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Compare each photon energy with the work function $\phi$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: For an allowed event use $K_{\max}=E_\gamma-\phi$; below threshold there is no emission.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that kinetic energy is never assigned a negative physical value.

commonErrors.description: For the $2.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ photon, $K_{\max}=-0.20\,\mathrm{eV}$, so an electron emerges with negative kinetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: A negative algebraic remainder means the photon is below threshold and no photoelectron is emitted.

commonErrors.description: Greater light intensity lets the $2.10\,\mathrm{eV}$ photons combine until one electron escapes.
commonErrors.consequence: In the ordinary one-photon regime, intensity changes event rate but not the energy of each photon.

problems.solution: At $2.10\,\mathrm{eV}<2.30\,\mathrm{eV}$ there is no photoemission. At $2.70\,\mathrm{eV}$ emission occurs and $K_{\max}=2.70-2.30=0.40\,\mathrm{eV}$. The threshold is an energy condition per photon, and a negative remainder is interpreted as no event.
problems.flawedProof: Einstein's equation gives $K_{\max}=2.10-2.30=-0.20\,\mathrm{eV}$ for the first light source. Therefore an electron is emitted in both cases, but the first group leaves with negative kinetic energy.

problems.title: Mass scaling of matter waves
problems.objective: Analyze mass scaling of matter waves from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A proton and an electron have the same nonrelativistic speed. Which has the larger de Broglie wavelength, and by what factor? Use $m_p/m_e=1836$.
problems.strategy: First: Write $\lambda=h/(mv)$ for each particle. Next: Form the ratio $\lambda_e/\lambda_p$ at equal speed. Finally: Check the limiting idea that greater momentum means shorter wavelength.
hints: Write $\lambda=h/(mv)$ for each particle.
Form the ratio $\lambda_e/\lambda_p$ at equal speed.
Check the limiting idea that greater momentum means shorter wavelength.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Write $\lambda=h/(mv)$ for each particle.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Form the ratio $\lambda_e/\lambda_p$ at equal speed.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check the limiting idea that greater momentum means shorter wavelength.

commonErrors.description: The proton wavelength is $1836$ times larger because the proton is heavier.
commonErrors.consequence: At equal speed the heavier particle has greater momentum and therefore a shorter wavelength.

commonErrors.description: The wavelengths are equal because both particles move at the same speed.
commonErrors.consequence: Matter wavelength depends on momentum, which includes mass, not speed alone.

problems.solution: $\lambda_e/\lambda_p=(h/m_ev)/(h/m_pv)=m_p/m_e=1836$. Thus the electron wavelength is $1836$ times the proton wavelength. This agrees with $\lambda\propto1/p$: at equal speed the proton carries much greater momentum.
problems.flawedProof: At the same speed the proton is $1836$ times heavier, so I multiply the electron wavelength by $1836$. Hence $\lambda_p=1836\lambda_e$, and the proton has the longer matter wave.

problems.title: Stopping potential for ultraviolet light
problems.objective: Analyze stopping potential for ultraviolet light from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: Light of wavelength $250\,\mathrm{nm}$ illuminates a metal with work function $2.20\,\mathrm{eV}$. Find the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy and the stopping-potential magnitude. Use $hc=1240\,\mathrm{eV\,nm}$.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the photon energy from $E_\gamma=hc/\lambda$ in electronvolts. Next: Subtract the work function to obtain $K_{\max}$. Finally: Use $eV_s=K_{\max}$ and distinguish the positive magnitude $V_s$ from electrode-polarity conventions.
permittedResults: One electronvolt is the energy an elementary charge gains across one volt.
hints: Compute the photon energy from $E_\gamma=hc/\lambda$ in electronvolts.
Subtract the work function to obtain $K_{\max}$.
Use $eV_s=K_{\max}$ and distinguish the positive magnitude $V_s$ from electrode-polarity conventions.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Compute the photon energy from $E_\gamma=hc/\lambda$ in electronvolts.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Subtract the work function to obtain $K_{\max}$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Use $eV_s=K_{\max}$ and distinguish the positive magnitude $V_s$ from electrode-polarity conventions.

commonErrors.description: Uses $K_{\max}=\phi-hc/\lambda=-2.76\,\mathrm{eV}$ and calls the stopping potential negative in magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy balance is reversed; the emitted electron receives photon energy left after paying the work function.

commonErrors.description: Divides the kinetic energy in electronvolts by $1.602\times10^{-19}$ to get volts.
commonErrors.consequence: Numerically, an electron energy in electronvolts corresponds to the same stopping-potential magnitude in volts.

problems.solution: $E_\gamma=1240/250=4.96\,\mathrm{eV}$. Hence $K_{\max}=4.96-2.20=2.76\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $V_s=2.76\,\mathrm V$ in magnitude. A retarding electrode polarity is chosen so that the electric potential energy increase is $eV_s$.
problems.flawedProof: I subtract the photon energy from the work function: $K_{\max}=\phi-hc/\lambda=2.20-4.96=-2.76\,\mathrm{eV}$. Therefore the stopping-potential magnitude is $-2.76\,\mathrm V$.

problems.title: Compton wavelength shift at right angles
problems.objective: Analyze compton wavelength shift at right angles from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: An x-ray photon scatters from a nearly free electron through $90.0^\circ$. Find the wavelength increase. Use $h/(m_ec)=2.426\,\mathrm{pm}$.
problems.strategy: First: Use the Compton shift formula with the photon scattering angle $\theta$. Next: Evaluate $1-\cos90.0^\circ$ and retain wavelength units. Finally: Check that the shift lies between zero for forward scattering and twice the Compton wavelength for backscattering.
hints: Use the Compton shift formula with the photon scattering angle $\theta$.
Evaluate $1-\cos90.0^\circ$ and retain wavelength units.
Check that the shift lies between zero for forward scattering and twice the Compton wavelength for backscattering.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use the Compton shift formula with the photon scattering angle $\theta$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Evaluate $1-\cos90.0^\circ$ and retain wavelength units.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the shift lies between zero for forward scattering and twice the Compton wavelength for backscattering.

commonErrors.description: Uses $1+\cos\theta$ and obtains the same maximum shift for forward scattering.
commonErrors.consequence: Forward scattering must give zero wavelength change, so the angular factor has the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Uses the electron recoil angle in place of the photon scattering angle without deriving a relation between them.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated Compton formula is written in terms of the outgoing photon's angle.

problems.solution: $\Delta\lambda=(2.426\,\mathrm{pm})(1-\cos90.0^\circ)=2.426\,\mathrm{pm}$. This is between the correct endpoint values $0$ at $0^\circ$ and $4.852\,\mathrm{pm}$ at $180^\circ$.
problems.flawedProof: I use $\Delta\lambda=[h/(m_ec)](1+\cos\theta)$. At $90^\circ$ this gives $2.426\,\mathrm{pm}$, and at $0^\circ$ it predicts the maximum shift $4.852\,\mathrm{pm}$.

problems.title: Minimum momentum spread from localization
problems.objective: Analyze minimum momentum spread from localization from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: An electron is prepared with position standard deviation $\Delta x=0.100\,\mathrm{nm}$. Find the minimum allowed $\Delta p_x$ and the corresponding nonrelativistic speed-spread estimate $\Delta p_x/m_e$. Use $\hbar=1.055\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
problems.strategy: First: Convert $\Delta x$ to metres and saturate $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$ for the minimum. Next: Divide the resulting momentum spread by $m_e$ for the nonrelativistic estimate. Finally: Compare the speed spread with $c$ to audit the approximation.
hints: Convert $\Delta x$ to metres and saturate $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$ for the minimum.
Divide the resulting momentum spread by $m_e$ for the nonrelativistic estimate.
Compare the speed spread with $c$ to audit the approximation.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Convert $\Delta x$ to metres and saturate $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2$ for the minimum.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Divide the resulting momentum spread by $m_e$ for the nonrelativistic estimate.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Compare the speed spread with $c$ to audit the approximation.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\Delta p_x=2\hbar\Delta x$.
commonErrors.consequence: The uncertainty product requires division by the position spread, and the proposed expression also has incorrect dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Treats $0.100\,\mathrm{nm}$ as $0.100\,\mathrm m$.
commonErrors.consequence: The missing factor of $10^{-9}$ changes the bound by nine orders of magnitude.

problems.solution: $\Delta x=1.00\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m$, so $\Delta p_{x,\min}=\hbar/(2\Delta x)=5.28\times10^{-25}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. The speed-spread estimate is $5.28\times10^{-25}/(9.109\times10^{-31})=5.79\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, only $1.93\times10^{-3}c$, so the nonrelativistic estimate is consistent.
problems.flawedProof: I rearrange the uncertainty relation as $\Delta p_x=2\hbar\Delta x$. With $\Delta x=1.00\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m$, I obtain $\Delta p_x=2.11\times10^{-44}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.

problems.title: Energy levels in a nanometre box
problems.objective: Analyze energy levels in a nanometre box from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: An electron is confined in a one-dimensional infinite square well of width $L=1.00\,\mathrm{nm}$. Find $E_1$, $E_2$, and the photon energy for the transition $2\to1$. Use $h=6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm J$.
problems.strategy: First: Use $E_n=n^2h^2/(8m_eL^2)$ with $L$ in metres. Next: Evaluate $E_1$, use $E_2=4E_1$, and take their difference. Finally: Check that the ground energy is nonzero and that the emitted photon carries a positive energy.
permittedResults: For a one-dimensional infinite well, $E_n=n^2h^2/(8mL^2)$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$.
hints: Use $E_n=n^2h^2/(8m_eL^2)$ with $L$ in metres.
Evaluate $E_1$, use $E_2=4E_1$, and take their difference.
Check that the ground energy is nonzero and that the emitted photon carries a positive energy.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use $E_n=n^2h^2/(8m_eL^2)$ with $L$ in metres.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Evaluate $E_1$, use $E_2=4E_1$, and take their difference.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the ground energy is nonzero and that the emitted photon carries a positive energy.

commonErrors.description: Sets $n=0$ for the ground state and obtains zero ground-state energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The infinite-well boundary conditions admit only positive integer $n$; the identically zero function is not a state.

commonErrors.description: Uses $E_2=2E_1$ because the quantum number doubles.
commonErrors.consequence: Infinite-well energies scale as $n^2$, not as $n$.

problems.solution: $L=1.00\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm m$ gives $E_1=h^2/(8m_eL^2)=6.02\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm J=0.376\,\mathrm{eV}$. Thus $E_2=1.504\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $E_\gamma=E_2-E_1=1.128\,\mathrm{eV}$. The nonzero ground energy is required by confinement.
problems.flawedProof: The quantum number starts at zero, so $E_0=0$ is the ground-state energy. I then call the listed $n=1$ level the first excited state and conclude that an electron can remain motionless in the box.

problems.title: Ground-state probability in the middle half
problems.objective: Analyze ground-state probability in the middle half from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A particle in the ground state of a one-dimensional infinite well $0<x<L$ has $\psi_1(x)=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(\pi x/L)$. Find $P(L/4<x<3L/4)$ exactly and numerically.
problems.strategy: First: Integrate $(2/L)\sin^2(\pi x/L)$ over the requested interval. Next: Use $\sin^2u=(1-\cos2u)/2$ and evaluate both endpoints carefully. Finally: Check that the answer lies between zero and one and exceeds one half because the density peaks at the centre.
permittedResults: Probabilities are integrals of $|\psi|^2$ over the measurement region.
hints: Integrate $(2/L)\sin^2(\pi x/L)$ over the requested interval.
Use $\sin^2u=(1-\cos2u)/2$ and evaluate both endpoints carefully.
Check that the answer lies between zero and one and exceeds one half because the density peaks at the centre.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Integrate $(2/L)\sin^2(\pi x/L)$ over the requested interval.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Use $\sin^2u=(1-\cos2u)/2$ and evaluate both endpoints carefully.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the answer lies between zero and one and exceeds one half because the density peaks at the centre.

commonErrors.description: Uses interval length alone and reports $P=1/2$ because the region occupies half the box.
commonErrors.consequence: The ground-state density is not uniform; it is greatest near $x=L/2$.

commonErrors.description: Integrates $\psi_1$ rather than $|\psi_1|^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The Born rule uses the modulus-squared density.

problems.solution: Using $\int(2/L)\sin^2(\pi x/L)dx=x/L-\sin(2\pi x/L)/(2\pi)$, the endpoint difference is $P=1/2+1/\pi=0.8183$. It is greater than $1/2$, as expected because the ground-state density is concentrated around the middle.
problems.flawedProof: The interval from $L/4$ to $3L/4$ occupies exactly half of the box. Therefore its probability is $P=(3L/4-L/4)/L=1/2$, independent of the shape of $|\psi_1|^2$.

problems.title: Exponential tunnelling estimate
problems.objective: Analyze exponential tunnelling estimate from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: Electrons of kinetic energy $E=2.00\,\mathrm{eV}$ encounter a rectangular barrier of height $V_0=5.00\,\mathrm{eV}$ and width $a=0.200\,\mathrm{nm}$. Estimate the transmission with $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$ and $\kappa=\sqrt{2m_e(V_0-E)}/\hbar$. Use $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $\hbar=1.055\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm J$.
problems.strategy: First: Convert the barrier excess $V_0-E$ to joules before finding $\kappa$. Next: Form the dimensionless exponent $2\kappa a$ and evaluate $T$. Finally: Check that $0<T<1$ and that increasing either width or barrier excess decreases transmission.
permittedResults: For a sufficiently opaque rectangular barrier, $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$ with $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$.
hints: Convert the barrier excess $V_0-E$ to joules before finding $\kappa$.
Form the dimensionless exponent $2\kappa a$ and evaluate $T$.
Check that $0<T<1$ and that increasing either width or barrier excess decreases transmission.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Convert the barrier excess $V_0-E$ to joules before finding $\kappa$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Form the dimensionless exponent $2\kappa a$ and evaluate $T$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that $0<T<1$ and that increasing either width or barrier excess decreases transmission.

commonErrors.description: Uses $V_0$ instead of $V_0-E$ in $\kappa$ while claiming the electron's incident energy is irrelevant.
commonErrors.consequence: The evanescent decay is controlled by the energy deficit inside the barrier.

commonErrors.description: Leaves $a$ in nanometres when multiplying by $\kappa$ in inverse metres.
commonErrors.consequence: The exponent then is not dimensionless and the numerical transmission is meaningless.

problems.solution: $V_0-E=3.00\,\mathrm{eV}=4.806\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm J$. Thus $\kappa=\sqrt{2(9.109\times10^{-31})(4.806\times10^{-19})}/(1.055\times10^{-34})=8.87\times10^9\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Therefore $2\kappa a=3.55$ and $T\approx e^{-3.55}=2.88\times10^{-2}$. The exponential decreases with either $a$ or $V_0-E$.
problems.flawedProof: Inside the barrier I take $\kappa=\sqrt{2m_eV_0}/\hbar$, because only the barrier height sets the decay. I therefore use $T=e^{-2a\sqrt{2m_eV_0}/\hbar}$ without including the incident energy.

problems.title: Bohr orbit scales at n equals three
problems.objective: Analyze bohr orbit scales at n equals three from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, find the radius, electron speed, and energy for $n=3$. Use $a_0=5.292\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm m$, $v_1=2.188\times10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $E_1=-13.60\,\mathrm{eV}$.

hints: Use the Bohr scalings $r_n=n^2a_0$, $v_n=v_1/n$, and $E_n=E_1/n^2$.
Substitute $n=3$ and retain the negative sign of the bound-state energy.

commonErrors.description: Computes $[\hat p,\hat x]=i\hbar$ and assigns that sign to $[\hat x,\hat p]$.
commonErrors.consequence: Reversing commutator order changes its sign.

problems.solution: $\hat x\hat p\psi=-i\hbar x\psi'$, while $\hat p\hat x\psi=-i\hbar(x\psi)'=-i\hbar(\psi+x\psi')$. Thus $[\hat x,\hat p]\psi=i\hbar\psi$, so $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar$. Robertson then gives $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\tfrac12|i\hbar|=\hbar/2$.
problems.flawedProof: I differentiate $x\psi$ as $(x\psi)'=x\psi'$. Then $\hat x\hat p\psi$ and $\hat p\hat x\psi$ are identical, so $[\hat x,\hat p]=0$ and there is no uncertainty lower bound.

problems.title: Hydrogen degeneracy at n equals four
problems.objective: Analyze hydrogen degeneracy at n equals four from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: Ignoring electron spin, fine structure, and external fields, count the distinct hydrogen orbital states with principal quantum number $n=4$. List the allowed $l$ values and explain the count. Then include the two spin projections.
problems.strategy: First: For fixed $n$, list $l=0,1,\ldots,n-1$. Next: For each $l$, count $2l+1$ values of $m_l$ and sum them. Finally: Double only after the orbital count to include spin, and state the idealizations under which these states share an energy.
hints: For fixed $n$, list $l=0,1,\ldots,n-1$.
For each $l$, count $2l+1$ values of $m_l$ and sum them.
Double only after the orbital count to include spin, and state the idealizations under which these states share an energy.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: For fixed $n$, list $l=0,1,\ldots,n-1$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: For each $l$, count $2l+1$ values of $m_l$ and sum them.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Double only after the orbital count to include spin, and state the idealizations under which these states share an energy.

commonErrors.description: Counts four states because only the four values of $l$ matter.
commonErrors.consequence: Each $l$ multiplet contains $2l+1$ distinct magnetic substates.

commonErrors.description: Includes electron spin by adding two rather than multiplying by two.
commonErrors.consequence: Every orbital state can carry either of two spin projections.

problems.solution: For $n=4$, $l=0,1,2,3$, contributing $1,3,5,7$ values of $m_l$. The orbital total is $1+3+5+7=16=n^2$. Including $m_s=\pm1/2$ gives $32$ one-electron states. Equality of their nonrelativistic Coulomb energies assumes no fine structure or external field.
problems.flawedProof: For $n=4$, the allowed values are $l=0,1,2,3$. I count those four labels as four orbital states and then double for spin, giving eight states in total.

problems.title: Geometry of a measured angular-momentum state
problems.objective: Analyze geometry of a measured angular-momentum state from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A particle is in the simultaneous eigenstate $|l=2,m=-1\rangle$. Find the possible measured values of $L^2$ and $L_z$, and compute the semiclassical direction-cosine ratio $L_z/\sqrt{L^2}$.
problems.strategy: First: Use the eigenvalues $L^2=l(l+1)\hbar^2$ and $L_z=m\hbar$. Next: Substitute $l=2$ and $m=-1$ and form the requested ratio. Finally: Check that the magnitude of the ratio is at most one and do not replace $\sqrt{l(l+1)}$ by $l$.
hints: Use the eigenvalues $L^2=l(l+1)\hbar^2$ and $L_z=m\hbar$.
Substitute $l=2$ and $m=-1$ and form the requested ratio.
Check that the magnitude of the ratio is at most one and do not replace $\sqrt{l(l+1)}$ by $l$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use the eigenvalues $L^2=l(l+1)\hbar^2$ and $L_z=m\hbar$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Substitute $l=2$ and $m=-1$ and form the requested ratio.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that the magnitude of the ratio is at most one and do not replace $\sqrt{l(l+1)}$ by $l$.

commonErrors.description: Uses $L=l\hbar$ and reports the ratio $m/l=-1/2$.
commonErrors.consequence: Quantum angular-momentum magnitude is $\sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$, not $l\hbar$.

commonErrors.description: Reports multiple possible $L_z$ values even though the state already has a definite $m$.
commonErrors.consequence: A measurement in an eigenstate returns its eigenvalue with probability one.

problems.solution: $L^2=2(3)\hbar^2=6\hbar^2$ and $L_z=-\hbar$, each with certainty. Therefore $L_z/\sqrt{L^2}=-1/\sqrt6=-0.408$. Its magnitude is below one, and the result reflects the quantum magnitude $\sqrt{l(l+1)}\hbar$.
problems.flawedProof: The angular-momentum magnitude is $L=l\hbar=2\hbar$. Therefore $L_z/L=m/l=-1/2$, while $L^2$ is simply $4\hbar^2$.

problems.title: Three sequential Stern-Gerlach filters
problems.objective: Analyze three sequential stern-gerlach filters from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A beam of spin-$1/2$ particles is prepared in $|+z\rangle$. It passes through a filter selecting $+x$, then through a filter selecting $+z$. Find the fraction of the original beam transmitted by both filters and the final spin state. Assume ideal filters and ignore particle loss other than rejected spin channels.
problems.strategy: First: Use $|\langle+x|+z\rangle|^2$ for transmission through the first filter. Next: After successful $+x$ selection, treat the state as $|+x\rangle$ before the $+z$ filter. Finally: Multiply conditional probabilities for the surviving fraction and identify the postselected final state.
permittedResults: For orthogonal spin axes, either outcome has probability $1/2$ from an eigenstate of the other axis.
hints: Use $|\langle+x|+z\rangle|^2$ for transmission through the first filter.
After successful $+x$ selection, treat the state as $|+x\rangle$ before the $+z$ filter.
Multiply conditional probabilities for the surviving fraction and identify the postselected final state.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use $|\langle+x|+z\rangle|^2$ for transmission through the first filter.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: After successful $+x$ selection, treat the state as $|+x\rangle$ before the $+z$ filter.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Multiply conditional probabilities for the surviving fraction and identify the postselected final state.

commonErrors.description: Claims the final $+z$ filter transmits every survivor because the beam originally began in $|+z\rangle$.
commonErrors.consequence: The intervening $+x$ measurement changes the postselected state and erases definite $z$ spin.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two one-half probabilities and obtains a transmitted fraction of one.
commonErrors.consequence: Sequential conditional probabilities multiply along the selected path.

problems.solution: The $+x$ filter transmits $1/2$ of the original beam and prepares those survivors in $|+x\rangle$. The subsequent $+z$ probability is again $1/2$, so the total transmitted fraction is $(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$. Particles leaving the final filter are in $|+z\rangle$.
problems.flawedProof: The first filter transmits half the beam, but the particles were originally prepared in $|+z\rangle$. The final $+z$ filter therefore transmits every survivor, so the total fraction is $1/2$.

problems.title: Bloch direction of a complex spin state
problems.objective: Analyze bloch direction of a complex spin state from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A normalized spin state is $|\psi\rangle=(\sqrt3/2)|+z\rangle+(i/2)|-z\rangle$. Find $\langle S_x\rangle$, $\langle S_y\rangle$, and $\langle S_z\rangle$, then find the probability of obtaining $+\hbar/2$ in a measurement of $S_y$.
problems.strategy: First: Write the spinor coefficients $a=\sqrt3/2$ and $b=i/2$ in the $z$ basis. Next: Use $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}(a^*b)$, $\langle\sigma_y\rangle=2\operatorname{Im}(a^*b)$, and $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=|a|^2-|b|^2$. Finally: Convert the $y$ component to $P(+y)=[1+\langle\sigma_y\rangle]/2$ and check the Bloch-vector length.
permittedResults: For a pure spin-$1/2$ state, the Bloch vector has unit length.
hints: Write the spinor coefficients $a=\sqrt3/2$ and $b=i/2$ in the $z$ basis.
Use $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}(a^*b)$, $\langle\sigma_y\rangle=2\operatorname{Im}(a^*b)$, and $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=|a|^2-|b|^2$.
Convert the $y$ component to $P(+y)=[1+\langle\sigma_y\rangle]/2$ and check the Bloch-vector length.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Write the spinor coefficients $a=\sqrt3/2$ and $b=i/2$ in the $z$ basis.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Use $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}(a^*b)$, $\langle\sigma_y\rangle=2\operatorname{Im}(a^*b)$, and $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=|a|^2-|b|^2$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Convert the $y$ component to $P(+y)=[1+\langle\sigma_y\rangle]/2$ and check the Bloch-vector length.

commonErrors.description: Ignores the factor $i$ and treats both amplitudes as real, producing a nonzero $\langle S_x\rangle$ instead of $\langle S_y\rangle$.
commonErrors.consequence: The relative complex phase determines the transverse Bloch-vector direction.

commonErrors.description: Sets $P(+y)=\langle S_y\rangle$.
commonErrors.consequence: An expectation value with units of angular momentum is not itself a probability.

problems.solution: $a^*b=i\sqrt3/4$, so $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=0$, $\langle\sigma_y\rangle=\sqrt3/2$, and $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=1/2$. Hence $(\langle S_x\rangle,\langle S_y\rangle,\langle S_z\rangle)=(\hbar/2)(0,\sqrt3/2,1/2)$. Also $P(+y)=(2+\sqrt3)/4=0.933$. The Bloch-vector length is one.
problems.flawedProof: I drop the factor $i$ and use real coefficients $a=\sqrt3/2$ and $b=1/2$. This gives $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=\sqrt3/2$, $\langle\sigma_y\rangle=0$, and places the transverse spin along $x$.

problems.title: Electron wavelength after acceleration
problems.objective: Analyze electron wavelength after acceleration from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of $150\,\mathrm V$. Find its nonrelativistic de Broglie wavelength. Use $h=6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$, $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$. Check against the electron rest energy $511\,\mathrm{keV}$.
problems.strategy: First: Set the gained kinetic energy equal to $eV$ and use $p=\sqrt{2m_e eV}$. Next: Evaluate $\lambda=h/p$ in metres and nanometres. Finally: Compare $150\,\mathrm{eV}$ with $511\,\mathrm{keV}$ to justify the approximation.
permittedResults: A charge of magnitude $e$ accelerated from rest through voltage magnitude $V$ gains kinetic energy $eV$.
hints: Set the gained kinetic energy equal to $eV$ and use $p=\sqrt{2m_e eV}$.
Evaluate $\lambda=h/p$ in metres and nanometres.
Compare $150\,\mathrm{eV}$ with $511\,\mathrm{keV}$ to justify the approximation.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Set the gained kinetic energy equal to $eV$ and use $p=\sqrt{2m_e eV}$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Evaluate $\lambda=h/p$ in metres and nanometres.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Compare $150\,\mathrm{eV}$ with $511\,\mathrm{keV}$ to justify the approximation.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p=m_e eV$ as though energy were a speed.
commonErrors.consequence: The expression has incorrect dimensions; nonrelativistically $p=\sqrt{2mK}$.

commonErrors.description: Uses $K=150\,\mathrm{keV}$ instead of $150\,\mathrm{eV}$ and rejects the nonrelativistic approximation.
commonErrors.consequence: The voltage gives $150$ electronvolts, three orders of magnitude below a kiloelectronvolt.

problems.solution: $p=\sqrt{2(9.109\times10^{-31})(1.602\times10^{-19})(150)}=6.62\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Thus $\lambda=6.626\times10^{-34}/(6.62\times10^{-24})=1.00\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm m=0.100\,\mathrm{nm}$. Since $150\,\mathrm{eV}/511\,\mathrm{keV}=2.94\times10^{-4}$, relativistic corrections are negligible.
problems.flawedProof: The gained energy is $eV$, so I write the momentum as $p=m_e eV$. Substitution gives $p=2.19\times10^{-47}\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and an enormous wavelength $\lambda=h/p$.

problems.title: Thermal scale at the solar spectrum peak
problems.objective: Analyze thermal scale at the solar spectrum peak from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: Approximate the Sun as a blackbody at $T=5800\,\mathrm K$. Use Wien's law to find the wavelength of peak spectral radiance per unit wavelength, then find the photon energy at that wavelength and compare it with $k_BT$. Use $b=2.898\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$, $hc=1240\,\mathrm{eV\,nm}$, and $k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV/K}$.
problems.strategy: First: Use $\lambda_{\max}T=b$ and convert the peak wavelength to nanometres. Next: Evaluate $E_\gamma=hc/\lambda_{\max}$ and $k_BT$ in electronvolts. Finally: Compare the two scales and remember that a spectral peak depends on whether wavelength or frequency density is plotted.
permittedResults: For spectral radiance per unit wavelength, $\lambda_{\max}T=b$.
hints: Use $\lambda_{\max}T=b$ and convert the peak wavelength to nanometres.
Evaluate $E_\gamma=hc/\lambda_{\max}$ and $k_BT$ in electronvolts.
Compare the two scales and remember that a spectral peak depends on whether wavelength or frequency density is plotted.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Use $\lambda_{\max}T=b$ and convert the peak wavelength to nanometres.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Evaluate $E_\gamma=hc/\lambda_{\max}$ and $k_BT$ in electronvolts.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Compare the two scales and remember that a spectral peak depends on whether wavelength or frequency density is plotted.

commonErrors.description: Equates the peak photon energy to exactly $k_BT$ without using Wien's law.
commonErrors.consequence: The wavelength-spectrum maximum occurs at a dimensionless energy of order five, not exactly one.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the frequency-spectrum and wavelength-spectrum peaks must identify the same photons.
commonErrors.consequence: Changing variables changes the density and therefore the numerical location of its maximum.

problems.solution: $\lambda_{\max}=2.898\times10^{-3}/5800=4.997\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm m=500\,\mathrm{nm}$. The corresponding photon energy is $1240/499.7=2.48\,\mathrm{eV}$, while $k_BT=(8.617\times10^{-5})(5800)=0.500\,\mathrm{eV}$. Thus $E_\gamma/(k_BT)=4.97$, appropriate for the wavelength-spectrum peak.
problems.flawedProof: A typical blackbody photon at the spectrum peak must have exactly $E_\gamma=k_BT$. At $5800\,\mathrm K$ this is $0.500\,\mathrm{eV}$, corresponding to $\lambda=2480\,\mathrm{nm}$, which I call the solar peak.

problems.title: Planck oscillator versus equipartition
problems.objective: Analyze planck oscillator versus equipartition from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A quantum harmonic mode has $\hbar\omega/(k_BT)=2.00$. Ignoring zero-point energy, compute its mean excitation energy $\langle E\rangle=\hbar\omega/[e^{\hbar\omega/(k_BT)}-1]$ as a multiple of $\hbar\omega$, and compare it with the classical value $k_BT$.
problems.strategy: First: Insert the dimensionless ratio two into the Bose mean-energy expression. Next: Rewrite $k_BT$ as $(\hbar\omega)/2$ for the comparison. Finally: Check that quantum suppression is expected when the level spacing exceeds the thermal scale.
permittedResults: For a bosonic oscillator without zero-point energy, $\langle E\rangle=\hbar\omega/(e^{\hbar\omega/(k_BT)}-1)$.
hints: Insert the dimensionless ratio two into the Bose mean-energy expression.
Rewrite $k_BT$ as $(\hbar\omega)/2$ for the comparison.
Check that quantum suppression is expected when the level spacing exceeds the thermal scale.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Insert the dimensionless ratio two into the Bose mean-energy expression.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Rewrite $k_BT$ as $(\hbar\omega)/2$ for the comparison.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Check that quantum suppression is expected when the level spacing exceeds the thermal scale.

commonErrors.description: Uses equipartition and asserts $\langle E\rangle=k_BT=0.5\hbar\omega$ exactly at every temperature.
commonErrors.consequence: Equipartition is the high-temperature limit; discrete excitation suppresses the energy when $\hbar\omega$ is not small compared with $k_BT$.

commonErrors.description: Adds $\hbar\omega/2$ despite the instruction to ignore zero-point energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The requested mean is the thermal excitation energy only.

problems.solution: $\langle E\rangle/(\hbar\omega)=1/(e^2-1)=0.1565$. Classical equipartition gives $k_BT=0.500\hbar\omega$, over three times larger. The smaller quantum value is sensible because exciting one quantum costs $2k_BT$.
problems.flawedProof: Equipartition applies to the oscillator at every temperature, so $\langle E\rangle=k_BT$. Since $\hbar\omega/(k_BT)=2$, I obtain $\langle E\rangle=0.500\hbar\omega$ without the Planck denominator.

problems.title: Natural linewidth and quality factor
problems.objective: Analyze natural linewidth and quality factor from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement:
An atomic transition has vacuum wavelength $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ and excited-state lifetime $	au=10.0\,\mathrm{ns}$. Using the stated Lorentzian full-width estimate $\Delta
u=1/(2\pi	au)$, find $\Delta
u$ and the quality factor $Q=
u_0/\Delta
u$. Use $c=2.998	imes10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
problems.strategy: First: Compute the central frequency $\nu_0=c/\lambda$ with the wavelength in metres. Next: Evaluate the explicitly stated linewidth convention from the lifetime. Finally: Form the dimensionless quality factor and check that a long lifetime produces a narrow line and large $Q$.

Evaluate the explicitly stated linewidth convention from the lifetime.
Form the dimensionless quality factor and check that a long lifetime produces a narrow line and large $Q$.

Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Evaluate the explicitly stated linewidth convention from the lifetime.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\Delta\nu=2\pi\tau$.
commonErrors.consequence: The expression has units of time rather than frequency and reverses lifetime broadening.

commonErrors.description: Uses $600$ metres for the wavelength and obtains a radio-frequency transition.
commonErrors.consequence: The nanometre conversion is required for the optical central frequency.

problems.solution: $\nu_0=(2.998\times10^8)/(600\times10^{-9})=4.997\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The width is $\Delta\nu=1/[2\pi(10.0\times10^{-9})]=1.59\times10^7\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Thus $Q=3.14\times10^7$. The linewidth is tiny compared with the optical carrier, as expected for a nanosecond-lived state.
problems.flawedProof: I multiply rather than invert the lifetime relation and set $\Delta\nu=2\pi\tau$. For $\tau=10.0\,\mathrm{ns}$ this gives $\Delta\nu=6.28\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

problems.title: Reduced-mass isotope shift of Lyman alpha
problems.objective: Analyze reduced-mass isotope shift of lyman alpha from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: In a hydrogenic atom the Rydberg constant is proportional to the electron-nucleus reduced mass $\mu=m_eM/(m_e+M)$. Approximate $M_H/m_e=1836$ and $M_D/m_e=3672$. If hydrogen Lyman-$\alpha$ has wavelength $\lambda_H=121.567\,\mathrm{nm}$, estimate $\lambda_D$ and $\lambda_D-\lambda_H$, neglecting nuclear-size and relativistic effects.
problems.strategy: First: Write $\mu/m_e=1/(1+m_e/M)$ for each isotope. Next: Use transition wavenumber proportional to $\mu$, so wavelength is inversely proportional to $\mu$. Finally: Determine the sign of the shift before evaluating and check that it is small compared with the line wavelength.
permittedResults: For fixed quantum numbers, hydrogenic transition wavenumbers scale with the reduced mass.
hints: Write $\mu/m_e=1/(1+m_e/M)$ for each isotope.
Use transition wavenumber proportional to $\mu$, so wavelength is inversely proportional to $\mu$.
Determine the sign of the shift before evaluating and check that it is small compared with the line wavelength.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Write $\mu/m_e=1/(1+m_e/M)$ for each isotope.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Use transition wavenumber proportional to $\mu$, so wavelength is inversely proportional to $\mu$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Determine the sign of the shift before evaluating and check that it is small compared with the line wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the heavier deuterium nucleus increases wavelength because the whole atom is heavier.
commonErrors.consequence: A heavier nucleus makes $\mu$ closer to $m_e$, increasing the Rydberg wavenumber and shortening the wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full nuclear-mass ratio of two to predict that the deuterium wavelength is half the hydrogen wavelength.
commonErrors.consequence: The relevant reduced mass changes only by a few parts in $10^4$ because both nuclei are much heavier than the electron.

problems.solution: $\mu_H/m_e=1/(1+1/1836)$ and $\mu_D/m_e=1/(1+1/3672)$. Therefore $\lambda_D/\lambda_H=\mu_H/\mu_D=(1+1/3672)/(1+1/1836)=0.999728$. Hence $\lambda_D=121.534\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $\lambda_D-\lambda_H=-0.0331\,\mathrm{nm}$. The small negative shift has the expected sign.
problems.flawedProof: Deuterium is about twice as massive as hydrogen, so its transition wavelength should also double. I estimate $\lambda_D=2\lambda_H=243.134\,\mathrm{nm}$.

problems.title: Energy spread in a coherent box state
problems.objective: Analyze energy spread in a coherent box state from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A normalized state is $|\psi\rangle=\tfrac12|E_1\rangle+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}e^{i\phi}|E_3\rangle$, where $E_1=1.00\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $E_3=9.00\,\mathrm{eV}$. Find the possible energy outcomes, their probabilities, $\langle E\rangle$, and $\Delta E$. State whether any answer depends on $\phi$.
problems.strategy: First: Square the expansion-coefficient magnitudes to get energy probabilities. Next: Compute $\langle E\rangle$ and $\langle E^2\rangle$ as probability-weighted sums. Finally: Take the square root of the variance and explain why the relative phase does not affect an energy measurement.
permittedResults: For an observable eigenbasis, outcome probabilities are squared expansion magnitudes.
hints: Square the expansion-coefficient magnitudes to get energy probabilities.
Compute $\langle E\rangle$ and $\langle E^2\rangle$ as probability-weighted sums.
Take the square root of the variance and explain why the relative phase does not affect an energy measurement.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Square the expansion-coefficient magnitudes to get energy probabilities.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Compute $\langle E\rangle$ and $\langle E^2\rangle$ as probability-weighted sums.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Take the square root of the variance and explain why the relative phase does not affect an energy measurement.

commonErrors.description: Uses amplitudes $1/2$ and $\sqrt3/2$ directly as probabilities.
commonErrors.consequence: Probabilities are modulus squares, so the proposed values do not sum to one.

commonErrors.description: Averages the two energies equally because two eigenstates appear in the sum.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy outcomes carry unequal probabilities $1/4$ and $3/4$.

problems.solution: $P(E_1)=1/4$ and $P(E_3)=3/4$. Thus $\langle E\rangle=(1/4)(1)+(3/4)(9)=7.00\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $\langle E^2\rangle=(1/4)(1)^2+(3/4)(9)^2=61.0\,\mathrm{eV^2}$. Therefore $\Delta E=\sqrt{61-49}=\sqrt{12}=3.46\,\mathrm{eV}$. None depends on $\phi$ because energy probabilities use coefficient magnitudes.
problems.flawedProof: I read the expansion amplitudes directly as probabilities: $P(E_1)=1/2$ and $P(E_3)=\sqrt3/2$. I use these as weights even though their sum exceeds one.

problems.title: Radial probability of the hydrogen ground state
problems.objective: Analyze radial probability of the hydrogen ground state from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: The hydrogen $1s$ wavefunction is $\psi_{1s}(r)=(\pi a_0^3)^{-1/2}e^{-r/a_0}$. Derive the radial probability density $P_r(r)$, find its most probable radius for $r>0$, and calculate the probability that $r<a_0$.
problems.strategy: First: Multiply $|\psi|^2$ by the spherical shell volume factor $4\pi r^2$. Next: Differentiate the radial density, retaining the geometric $r^2$ factor, to locate its positive maximum. Finally: Integrate from zero to $a_0$ and check that the probability lies between zero and one.
permittedResults: For a spherically symmetric state, radial probability density is $P_r(r)=4\pi r^2|\psi(r)|^2$.
hints: Multiply $|\psi|^2$ by the spherical shell volume factor $4\pi r^2$.
Differentiate the radial density, retaining the geometric $r^2$ factor, to locate its positive maximum.
Integrate from zero to $a_0$ and check that the probability lies between zero and one.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the quantum or atomic model correctly: Multiply $|\psi|^2$ by the spherical shell volume factor $4\pi r^2$.
Executes the decisive calculation or argument: Differentiate the radial density, retaining the geometric $r^2$ factor, to locate its positive maximum.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Integrate from zero to $a_0$ and check that the probability lies between zero and one.

commonErrors.description: Maximizes $|\psi_{1s}(r)|^2$ alone and concludes the most probable radius is $r=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The probability of a radius includes the spherical-shell factor $4\pi r^2$; point density and radial density are different.

commonErrors.description: Treats $P_r(a_0)$, which has units of inverse length, as the probability inside $a_0$.
commonErrors.consequence: A probability over a radial interval requires integrating the radial density.

problems.solution: $P_r(r)=4r^2a_0^{-3}e^{-2r/a_0}$. For $r>0$, $d(\ln P_r)/dr=2/r-2/a_0=0$, so the maximum occurs at $r=a_0$. With $u=2r/a_0$, $P(r<a_0)=\tfrac12\int_0^2u^2e^{-u}du=1-5e^{-2}=0.3233$. The radial result differs from the point-density maximum at the origin.
problems.flawedProof: The point density is $|\psi_{1s}|^2\propto e^{-2r/a_0}$, which is largest at $r=0$. Therefore I state that the most probable measured radius is zero without a spherical-shell factor.

problems.title: Orthogonality of distinct bound energy states
problems.objective: Analyze orthogonality of distinct bound energy states from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: Let $\psi_m$ and $\psi_n$ be square-integrable bound eigenfunctions of the same one-dimensional Hamiltonian $\hat H=-(\hbar^2/2M)d^2/dx^2+V(x)$, where $V(x)$ is real, with distinct energies $E_m\ne E_n$. Prove that $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi_m^*(x)\psi_n(x)dx=0$. State exactly where the bound-state boundary condition is used.
problems.strategy: First: Multiply the $n$ eigenvalue equation by $\psi_m^*$ and the complex-conjugated $m$ equation by $\psi_n$. commonErrors.description: Finds a stationary point but never checks positivity or dimensional scaling.
commonErrors.consequence: The minimization and its physical interpretation require confirming the point is a true finite-width minimum with energy units.

problems.solution: $E(\alpha)=\hbar^2\alpha/(4m)+3\lambda/(4\alpha^2)$. Setting $dE/d\alpha=0$ gives $\alpha_*^3=6m\lambda/\hbar^2$, and $d^2E/d\alpha^2=9\lambda/(2\alpha^4)>0$. At the optimum the kinetic term is twice the potential term, so $E_{\mathrm{var}}=3\hbar^2\alpha_*/(8m)=\frac38 6^{1/3}\hbar^{4/3}\lambda^{1/3}m^{-2/3}$. The combination has energy dimensions and is an upper bound to the true ground energy.
problems.flawedProof: I minimize the positive terms independently. The kinetic term is smallest at $\alpha=0$, while the potential term is smallest as $\alpha\to\infty$; combining those separate minima gives $E_{\mathrm{var}}=0$.

problems.title: Detuned Rabi pulse limits
problems.objective: Analyze detuned rabi pulse limits from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: A two-level atom begins in $|g\rangle$ and is driven with on-resonance angular Rabi frequency $\Omega=2\pi(5.00\,\mathrm{MHz})$ and detuning $\Delta=2\pi(3.00\,\mathrm{MHz})$. In the rotating-wave model derive $P_e(t)=[\Omega^2/(\Omega^2+\Delta^2)]\sin^2[\tfrac12\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}t]$. Find the first maximum time and its value, and recover the resonant $\pi$-pulse limit as $\Delta\to0$.
problems.strategy: First: Diagonalize the rotating-frame Hamiltonian $(\hbar/2)(\Omega\sigma_x+\Delta\sigma_z)$ or exponentiate it using its effective-field magnitude. Next: Project the evolved initial ground state onto the excited state and evaluate the first sine-squared maximum. Finally: Take $\Delta\to0$ explicitly and check that the maximum becomes unity at $t=\pi/\Omega$.
permittedResults: For a constant vector $\mathbf a$, $e^{-i(\mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)t/2}=I\cos(at/2)-i(\mathbf a\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/a)\sin(at/2)$.

commonErrors.description: Uses $P_e=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)$ even off resonance and predicts unit excitation.
commonErrors.consequence: Detuning changes both the oscillation frequency and the maximum transfer amplitude.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two angular frequencies linearly instead of using $\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The effective drive and detuning are perpendicular components in the two-level Bloch Hamiltonian.

problems.solution: The effective angular frequency is $\Omega_R=\sqrt{\Omega^2+\Delta^2}$, and exponentiation gives $P_e=(\Omega^2/\Omega_R^2)\sin^2(\Omega_Rt/2)$. The first maximum occurs at $t=\pi/\Omega_R=1/[2\sqrt{(5.00\,\mathrm{MHz})^2+(3.00\,\mathrm{MHz})^2}]=85.7\,\mathrm{ns}$. Its value is $25/(25+9)=0.735$. For $\Delta\to0$, $P_e=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)$ and a $\pi$ pulse at $t=\pi/\Omega$ gives unit excitation.
problems.flawedProof: I ignore detuning and use $P_e(t)=\sin^2(\Omega t/2)$. It predicts complete excitation at $t=\pi/\Omega=100\,\mathrm{ns}$ despite the nonzero detuning.

problems.title: WKB spectrum of a quartic well
problems.objective: Analyze wkb spectrum of a quartic well from an explicit quantum or atomic model, with consistent SI units, stated assumptions, and a physical or limiting check.
problems.statement: For the one-dimensional potential $V(x)=\lambda x^4$ with $\lambda>0$, use the WKB condition $\int_{x_-}^{x_+}\sqrt{2m[E-V(x)]}dx=(n+1/2)\pi\hbar$. Let $C=\int_0^1\sqrt{1-u^4}du$. Derive an explicit formula for $E_n$ in terms of $C$, and extract the large-$n$ scaling. Check the dimensions and contrast the scaling with the harmonic oscillator.
problems.strategy: First: Find the turning points $x_\pm=\pm(E/\lambda)^{1/4}$ and use symmetry in the action integral. Next: Scale $x=(E/\lambda)^{1/4}u$ to factor all dimensional quantities outside the integral $C$. Finally: Solve the resulting power equation for $E_n$, verify energy dimensions, and compare the $n^{4/3}$ spacing trend with linear harmonic levels.
permittedResults: The two-turning-point WKB rule is the one stated in the problem.

commonErrors.description: Uses turning points $x_\pm=\pm E/\lambda$ and obtains an action with inconsistent dimensions.
commonErrors.consequence: Solving $E=\lambda x^4$ requires a fourth root.

commonErrors.description: Drops the factor of two from the symmetric interval and keeps the harmonic-oscillator scaling $E_n\propto n$.
commonErrors.consequence: Both turning-point halves contribute, and quartic scaling changes the power of energy in the action.

problems.solution: The turning point is $x_0=(E/\lambda)^{1/4}$. The action is $2\sqrt{2m}\int_0^{x_0}\sqrt{E-\lambda x^4}dx=2\sqrt{2m}E^{3/4}\lambda^{-1/4}C$. Equating this to $(n+1/2)\pi\hbar$ gives $E_n=[(n+1/2)\pi\hbar\lambda^{1/4}/(2\sqrt{2m}C)]^{4/3}$. Thus $E_n\propto(n+1/2)^{4/3}$, so spacings grow with $n$, unlike the constant harmonic-oscillator spacing. The combination scales as $\hbar^{4/3}\lambda^{1/3}m^{-2/3}$ and has energy dimensions.
problems.flawedProof: The turning points follow from $E=\lambda x$, so I take $x_\pm=\pm E/\lambda$. I integrate between those limits as though they bounded the allowed region and obtain an action based on that choice.
